title: Binary Search & Search on the Answer

chapters.title: Halve the range, find the first

scenes.say: I'm thinking of a number from one to a million. You get twenty guesses. By the end, you'll write binary search with no off by one bugs, then use it on problems that don't look like search.
Today you will do three things. Halve a range to find the first match. Write the loop with no off by one bugs. And search for an answer that isn't in any array.
lines: Halve a range to find a match
Search the answer, not an array

scenes.title: First value at least x
scenes.statement: Given a sorted array and a number x, find the first position holding a value at least x.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. Take this sorted array and x equal to seven. The first spot that's big enough: index three. And n can reach a million, so no scanning.

scenes.head: Scan versus halve
scenes.say: Coding tests love this one. Count the looks to find a value. Scanning a million sorted numbers can take a million looks. Binary search needs twenty. Same idea, even with no array at all.

scenes.head: The guessing game
scenes.say: Picture the game: a number from one to a hundred. You guess fifty. Too low, so it's fifty one to a hundred. Guess seventy five. Too high. Each guess halves the range, so a hundred numbers take seven guesses. A billion take thirty.

scenes.head: First value at least 7
scenes.say: Same halving, now on a sorted array. We want the first value at least seven. Lo is the earliest the answer could be: zero. Hi is the latest: six, past the end, in case none qualify. Middle is index three, value seven. Big enough, so hi moves to three, and the right cells are out. Middle is index one, value three. Too small, so lo jumps to two. Middle is index two, value five. Too small, so lo jumps to three. The answer is index three.

scenes.head: The template with no off-by-one
scenes.say: Here it is in C plus plus. Lo and hi start at the two ends. While lo is less than hi, take the middle, as lo plus half the gap. Too small? The answer is to the right, so lo becomes mid plus one. Otherwise mid might be the answer, so hi becomes mid. When they meet, lo is the answer.
Your turn. Same array, but now search for eight. Which index comes back? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Run it, including the edge
scenes.say: It's five, because nine at index five is the first value at least eight. Run it. Seven gives three. Eight gives five. Ten gives six, one past the end, because nothing is big enough.

scenes.head: Four traps interviewers watch
scenes.say: Four classic traps. Adding lo and hi can overflow, so use lo plus half the gap. Mixing loop styles can loop forever, so pick one template. If nothing qualifies, lo ends past the end, so check before reading. And on unsorted data, the answer is garbage.
rows: can loop forever: one template only

chapters.title: Search the answer, not the array

scenes.title: Smallest ship that works
scenes.statement: Ten packages must ship in order within five days. Find the smallest ship capacity that makes it.
scenes.say: New problem, and no sorted array in sight. Take weights one to ten, and five days. The smallest capacity that works is fifteen.

scenes.head: Smallest ship that works
scenes.say: Ask a yes or no question for each capacity. Does it ship all ten packages in five days? Twelve: no. Thirteen: no. Fourteen: no. Fifteen: yes. Sixteen: yes. Seventeen: yes. Bigger never hurts, so we want the first yes.

scenes.head: The yes or no check
scenes.say: How do we answer the question for one capacity? Walk the packages, loading the ship. If the next one would overflow, start a new day. Then add the package. At the end, fits means the days used are at most five. One pass, so O of n.

scenes.head: Binary search the capacity
scenes.say: Now binary search the capacity. Lo is ten, the heaviest package, since a ship must carry it. Hi is fifty five, the total, which always works. Middle is thirty two. Fits, so hi becomes thirty two. Middle twenty one fits too, so hi is twenty one. Middle fifteen fits, so hi is fifteen. Middle twelve fails, so lo is thirteen. Middle fourteen fails, so lo is fifteen. Smallest capacity: fifteen.

scenes.head: Same template, new question
scenes.say: Same template, different check. Lo is the heaviest package, hi is the total. Take the middle. If the ship fits, the answer is this or smaller, so hi becomes mid. If not, lo becomes mid plus one. And we return lo, exactly as before.
Your turn. Same ten packages, but only one day. What capacity does the search return? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Weights 1 to 10, one day. What does `ship` return?

scenes.head: One day means carry everything
scenes.say: Fifty five. One day means carrying everything, so capacity must be the total. Ten: no. Thirty: no. Fifty four leaves one package behind: no. Fifty five: yes. Fifty six: yes. Sixty: yes. Same shape: no, no, no, then yes forever.

scenes.head: What the search costs
scenes.say: Three things to watch. Cost: each check walks every package, and a billion takes about thirty checks. Big sums: the total may overflow int, so use long long. And the check must never flip back, or the search breaks.
rows: never flips back: yes stays yes

scenes.title: Does binary search apply?
scenes.statement: Two yes or no checks over candidate answers. Which one can we binary search for its first yes?

example.input: A: no no no yes yes · B: no yes no no yes

scenes.say: Last problem: when is this legal? Check A says no, no, no, yes, yes. Check B: no, yes, no, no, yes. Only A works. Let's see why B breaks.

scenes.head: Two problems, one shape
scenes.say: Look at what we did twice. For the array, the question was: is this value at least seven? For the ship: does this capacity fit? Both answer no, no, no, then yes, yes, yes. Find the first yes, and you're done. Searching candidate answers like this is search on the answer.
Now a check that breaks the rule: no, yes, no, no, yes. Run our template, lo zero, hi five. Which index comes back? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Checks: no, yes, no, no, yes. Template returns which index?

scenes.head: A check that flips back
scenes.say: Four. Watch it go wrong. Middle is index two: no, so lo jumps to three. Middle is index four: yes, so hi becomes four. Middle is index three: no, so lo jumps to four. It returns four, but the first yes was index one. The search never saw index one again.

scenes.head: The standard library version
scenes.say: For a sorted array, C plus plus already ships lower bound. It returns an iterator to the first element at least the value. Subtract begin to get the index. Three, same as ours. The search on the answer version, you still write yourself. And it needs sorted input.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How does binary search work? Keep a range that holds the answer and halve it. How fast? O of log n, so a billion items take thirty steps. Search on the answer? Find the first yes of a check that never flips back. Common mistakes? Overflowing mid, mixing loop templates, unsorted data.
rows: keep a range that holds the answer, halve it
O(log n): a billion items, 30 steps
What is search on the answer?
first yes of a check that never flips back
mid overflow, mixed templates, unsorted data

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these next. LeetCode thirty five, search insert position, is today's first template. LeetCode eight seventy five, Koko eating bananas, is search on the answer, new check. LeetCode four ten, split array largest sum, is the same idea, harder.
rows: search on the answer, new check

scenes.say: So say this. Binary search keeps a range that holds the answer and halves it. One template: lo less than hi, hi becomes mid, lo becomes mid plus one. And when a yes or no check never flips back, search the answer.
